_comment: Which session address belongs to which identity. Append-only.
Maintained by Keel.
agents/roster.json records which identities EXIST; the harness writes it.
This file records WHICH ADDRESS IS WHOSE, so a peer can be messaged by
identity rather than by guesswork: ListAgents names sessions things like
`rule30-b3` and `proofs-df`, those opaque names are the only thing
SendMessage accepts, and they say nothing about who is behind them.
This file does not record who is alive, on purpose. ListAgents knows that
authoritatively, from outside the process and without its cooperation, so
a stale row here is inert — nothing reads this file to decide who is
live.
TO FIND SOMEONE:
1. Call ListAgents. Those rows, and only those, are alive.
2. Look each one up here BY REF, not by session_name. A ref is unique
to a session; a name could be recycled by a later one, and matching
on name is the one way a stale row could deliver a real message to
the wrong process.
3. Cross-check `started` against the 'started Xh ago' ListAgents
prints. A matching ref with a start time that disagrees means ask,
not assume.
4. An unknown ref means an unknown identity. Ask who they are.
TO REGISTER YOURSELF, if you are a hand-started interactive identity
(Rowan, Keel, Cairn, and whoever comes next):
1. Call ListAgents once at session start. Its first line tells you your
own address: `This session is <name> [<ref>]`.
2. Append your row if your ref is not already present.
3. There is no step 3. Never delete a row, including your own. A
protocol step that runs at the end of an agent session is fiction —
sessions are killed, time out, or exhaust context far more often
than they exit cleanly.
Dispatched provers are deliberately absent. They are short-lived, the
scheduler already holds them as resources, and an inbound message
mid-proof would reach a worker as an instruction from outside its brief,
which is the one thing the brief exists to prevent.
